units.summary: Two students sitting before Rav use different metaphors to describe their exhaustion from study, illustrating the use of clean language.
Two students before Hillel (or Rabbi) ask a question about ritual purity, with one using more refined language than the other.
Three priests describe their small portions of showbread, and the one who uses a crude metaphor is investigated and found to be disqualified from service.
A gentile who was sneaking into the Temple to eat the Paschal lamb is caught and executed after Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira tricks him into exposing himself to the authorities.
When Rav Kahana dies, Rabbi Yehoshua is sent to check on him and reports the death to the Sages using a euphemism to avoid speaking directly of death.
Yoḥanan of Ḥakuk reports a wheat crop failure by praising the barley crop instead, demonstrating the use of clean language.
Upon Rav's arrival in Eretz Yisrael, he informs Rabbi Hiyya of the death of his parents through indirect questioning, leading Rabbi Hiyya to begin mourning rites.
A man's habitual use of a specific phrase leads the Sages to identify his tribal lineage.
A man's habitual praise of the seashore leads to the discovery of his Zebulunite ancestry.
Rava instructs the residents of Meḥoza to remove leaven belonging to gentile soldiers from their homes because the residents' financial responsibility for it makes it legally theirs.
Students living in the fields ask Rav if they are protected from robbers when traveling to and from the academy, and Rav guarantees their safety only for the trip there.

A maidservant in Rimon throws a stillborn into a pit, leading to a priestly inspection and a later rabbinic ruling on the ritual purity of the site. A maidservant threw a stillborn into a pit, and after a priest inspected it, the Sages ruled the area pure because scavengers likely removed the body.
A man deposits leaven with Yoḥanan Ḥakuka’a, which is then damaged by mice, leading Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi to rule on when and how it should be sold before Passover.
A Tanna recites a baraita before Rav Yehuda using the word 'on the back of' (al gav), and Rav Yehuda corrects him to say 'on the roof of' (al gag).
Rav Yirmeya raises a legal objection regarding the cost of wood, and an anonymous elder provides a legal distinction to resolve it.
Rav Huna bar Ḥinnana tells his son to pose a specific legal contradiction to Rav Pappa when he visits him.
Rav Ashi or Rav Kahana leaves the study hall to research a legal point and finds a Mishna that supports his view.
A reciter of traditions presents a legal chain of impurity transmission before Rav Sheshet.
Shimon HaAmmassoni, who had a system for interpreting every instance of the word 'et', abandoned his entire project when he reached the command to fear God, despite his students' protests.
A man threatened with death by a local lord if he does not kill another person seeks guidance from Rava, who rules that he must allow himself to be killed rather than murder.
Mar bar Rav Ashi discovers Ravina using prohibited orla olives to treat his daughter's fever and questions him, leading Ravina to justify the act as medicinal for a dangerous condition.
Rav Aḥa bar Ya’akov retracts a previous legal stance after considering a baraita regarding consecrated leaven.
Shmuel threatens pot merchants that he will publicize a lenient ruling allowing the use of old pots if they do not lower their prices after Passover.
An oven was smeared with meat grease and used for bread, leading Rava bar Ahilai to prohibit the bread entirely.
Ravina asks Rav Ashi how to prepare knives for Passover, and Rav Ashi reveals that he personally makes new ones, prompting Ravina to remark on the difference between the wealthy and the poor.
When asked about glazed vessels, Ameimar reports his physical observation of them 'sweating' liquid, leading him to prohibit them for Passover use.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua arrives and provides a legal explanation regarding the status of leavened bread.
Rava bar Mattana meets Abaye and Rav Ḥananya bar Avin and they debate the interpretation of a Mishna regarding teruma.
When Ravin travels to Eretz Yisrael and recites a law, Rabbi Yirmeya insults him and all Babylonians for their 'dark' and confused traditions.
While Rav Pappa and Rav Huna are debating a legal point, their noise wakes up Rav Idi bar Avin, who rebukes them and explains the reasoning behind Reish Lakish's ruling.
Rabbi Yehoshua instructs his sons on the specific nights of Passover when they should and should not knead their dough with milk.

Passage B describes a specific historical debate between Baitos ben Zonin and the Sages involving a concrete proposal (using a mold) and a definitive rejection, distinct from the father-son dialogue in Passage A.
Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok recounts a time he accompanied his father to Rabban Gamliel's house and observed them being served shaped matza, leading to a clarification of the law.

Rabbi Ilai travels between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua to resolve a legal question, eventually triggering Rabbi Eliezer to swear that the answer provided by Yehoshua was indeed the tradition from Sinai.
Rabbi Ile’a travels among the students of Rabbi Eliezer to find confirmation for a specific botanical ruling regarding Passover.
Ravina encounters Rav Aḥa searching for particularly bitter herbs and questions why he isn't using the preferred lettuce mentioned in the Mishna.
The Gemara begins to describe the specific practice of Mar son of Ravina's mother regarding the guarding of wheat for Passover.

After a boat of wheat capsized in the Hishta River, Rava initially permitted selling it to gentiles but changed his ruling to selling it in small measures to Jews after a challenge by Rabba bar Levai.
Rav Pappi permitted the Exilarch's cooks to mash roasted grain into food, but Rava objected because servants cannot be trusted to be careful.
Rav Mattana teaches that matza must be made with 'mayim shelanu' (water that rested), leading the people of Paphunya to mistakenly bring their jugs to him the next day demanding 'our water'.
A traveler from Eretz Yisrael visiting Babylonia asks for a dip for his meat but stops eating when he hears his hosts call the dip 'Kutach,' realizing it contains dairy.
The Sages present a legal theory to Rabbi Yirmeya and Rabbi Zeira, leading to a disagreement where Yirmeya accepts the logic while Zeira rejects it, sparking a debate.
Rabbi Eliezer bar Tzadok recounts how, when Passover eve fell on Shabbat in Yavne, Zonin announced the time to remove leaven and his father immediately went to do so.
Rabbi Yehoshua married a priest's daughter, fell ill, and attributed his illness to Aaron's displeasure with the match.
Passage B introduces new actors (Rav Idi bar Avin and Rav Pappa) and describes different positive outcomes (ordained sons and wealth) resulting from the same action of marrying a priest's daughter.
Rav Kahana attributes his exile to his marriage to a priest's daughter, though others argue his exile to a place of Torah was not a punishment.
Rabbi Akiva recounts to his students how, during his time as an ignoramus, he harbored such intense hatred for scholars that he wished to bite one like a donkey.
Rav Yosef has a near-death experience and returns to describe a world where social statuses are inverted and martyrs hold the highest place.
Rava intends to publicly explain the pronunciation of God's name but is stopped by an old man who points out that the name must remain hidden.

The sons of the residents of Beit She’an ask Rabbi Yoḥanan to release them from an arduous travel custom established by their fathers, but he refuses, citing the obligation to maintain ancestral traditions.
The residents of Ḥozai report their custom of separating challah from rice to Rav Yosef, who orders a public violation of the custom to correct them, leading to a legal challenge by Abaye.
Passage B describes a distinct event involving bathing in the city of Kabul, which follows the same narrative structure and features the same protagonists as the shoe-wearing incident in Passage A.
Yehuda and Hillel wore wide shoes in the city of Birei and were denounced by the local residents for violating their custom.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel sat on a merchant's stool in Akko and was denounced by the local residents.
Rabba bar bar Hana ate a specific type of fat in Babylonia and tried to hide it when colleagues visited, who then reported him to Abaye.

It narrates a specific interaction between Rabba bar bar Ḥana and his son involving a command and its justification, which is distinct from the subsequent story involving Rabbi Shimon ben Rabbi Yosei ben Lakonya.

Rabbi Yohanan ben Elazar recounts following his teacher into a garden where the teacher ate and shared prohibited sabbatical year cabbage. Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Elazar recounts following his teacher into a garden where the teacher ate Sabbatical year cabbage and instructed him on its permissibility.
Rav Natan bar Asya traveled on the second day of Shavuot based on his own calendar calculations, leading Rav Yosef to punish him and Abaye to debate the nature of that punishment.
While traveling from Israel to the Diaspora with Sabbatical wine, Rav Safra consults his companions on the law and concludes by praising Rav Huna's accuracy in transmitting traditions.
Rabbi Elai chopped down a palm tree with Sabbatical produce, leading to a legal analysis of his action.
Theodosius of Rome instituted the eating of roasted kids on Passover, prompting the Sages to send him a message threatening excommunication for misleading the people.
Ulla glares at Rabba bar bar Ḥana for a perceived misattribution of a teaching, leading to a tense exchange that Rav Yosef later characterizes using a verse from Proverbs.
Rav Yosef applies biblical verses to explain the psychological states of Ulla and Rabba bar bar Ḥana during their previous interaction.
At the conclusion of the first Shabbat, Adam is inspired to strike two stones together to create fire, for which he then recites a blessing.
Rav Pappa recounts how Rava tested the students with a legal contradiction regarding bringing vessels from a craftsman, and how they successfully resolved it.
The Mishna lists six customs of the people of Jericho and the Sages' reaction to them.
Passage B describes a distinct set of actions performed by the people of Jericho and the Sages' response, following the same structural formula as Passage A but involving different actors.
The Gemara lists six specific actions taken by King Hezekiah and the Sages' subsequent approval or disapproval of those deeds.
Jacob attempts to reveal the end of days to his sons but loses his prophetic inspiration, leading to a dialogue about their faith and the origin of a liturgical response.
Bohayan's son incorrectly designated vegetable pe'ah, so Bohayan intercepted the poor and replaced their haul with properly tithed produce.
To prevent corrupt priests from stealing animal hides, the owners consecrated them to the Temple, resulting in the Sanctuary being plated with gold.
Owners of sycamore trees in Jericho consecrated their timber to the Temple to prevent it from being seized by powerful men.
Passage B is a distinct lamentation and historical report involving different actors (the High Priestly houses) and a different setting than the sycamore incident in Jericho.
The Temple Courtyard is described as crying out to expel corrupt priests and welcome worthy ones.
Yissakhar of Kfar Barkai disrespects the king during a debate about sacrificial animals and, despite attempting to bribe his way out of the full punishment, ends up having both hands amputated.

Rabbi Simlai asks Rabbi Yoḥanan to teach him the Book of Genealogies in three months, leading Yoḥanan to throw a clod of dirt at him in rebuke, though Yoḥanan eventually answers a legal question once Simlai proves his worth.
During the time of Hillel, an elderly man was crushed to death by the massive crowds in the Temple courtyard on Passover.
King Agrippa orders a census of the Jewish people, which the High Priest conducts by collecting and counting one kidney from every Paschal lamb.

When the sons of Beteira forget whether the Paschal sacrifice overrides Shabbat, Hillel provides the answer, is appointed Nasi, and subsequently learns a forgotten detail from observing the intuitive actions of the common people.
The sons of Beteira question Hillel regarding the permissibility of uprooting a rabbinic decree in an unusual manner for a mitzvah, and he provides a ruling based on his tradition.
A Tanna recites a baraita before Rav Yitzḥak bar Avdimi, who points out a logical flaw in the sequence of the laws and suggests a corrected version.
On Shavuot, Rav Yosef orders a special calf to be prepared and remarks that without the Torah, he would be no different from any other man in the market.
Passage B features a different protagonist, Rav Sheshet, performing a distinct recurring action with its own specific dialogue and subsequent Gemara analysis.
During a legal debate, Rabbi Eliezer becomes so incensed by Rabbi Akiva's refutation that he curses him to die by slaughter, leading Akiva to beg for mercy.
Yehuda ben Dortai and his son moved to the south to distance themselves from Jerusalem and avoid the obligation of the Paschal lamb because they disagreed with the Sages' ruling.
Ravin arrives from Eretz Yisrael to Babylonia and reports a different version of Rabbi Elazar's legal ruling regarding peace-offerings.
Rav Yitzḥak bar Yosef finds Rabbi Abbahu in a crowd and asks him to resolve a contradiction in the Mishna, which Rabbi Abbahu does verbally.
Rabbi Zeira and Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzḥak sit together on a porch and discuss the legal consequences of accidental transgressions involving sacrificial meat and marital relations.
Rabban Gamliel questions Rabbi Tarfon about his absence from the study hall, and Tarfon explains he was occupied with the 'service' of eating teruma.
Rav Huna bar Ḥinnana instructs his son to pose a legal difficulty to Rabbi Zerika regarding liability for destructive acts on Shabbat.
The baraita records the habitual names Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Tarfon would use for the Paschal lamb based on its roasting method.
Ravin the Elder prepares a dove wrapped in dough for Rav, who then comments on whether he will eat the breading.
Rava visits the Exilarch's home and refuses to eat a breaded goose until he verifies the breading did not absorb blood.
Rabban Gamliel instructs his servant to roast the Paschal lamb on a metal grill, an incident cited to clarify the Mishna's ruling.
A young bird fell into a jug of dairy kamka, and Rav Ḥinnana permitted it, a ruling later praised by Rava.
A fish was roasted with meat, and Rava prohibited eating it with dairy because of the absorbed aroma.
Rabbi Yirmeya sends Rabbi Avin to challenge Rabbi Abbahu regarding a contradiction in Rabbi Yoḥanan's rulings, leading Abbahu to reveal that Yoḥanan had actually retracted his opinion.
Rav Huna son of Rav Natan visits Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak and defends his unconventional social etiquette regarding his title, seating, and drinking habits.
Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei visits a colleague and wittily defends his drinking a cup of wine in one gulp.

When Hosea fails to defend the sinning Israelites and suggests God replace them, God commands him to marry a prostitute to teach him the difficulty of casting away those one has 'acquired' and produced children with.

God orchestrates a personal family crisis for the prophet Hosea to teach him compassion for the Jewish people, leading Hosea to repent and successfully advocate for the nullification of a divine decree.
Rabbi Oshaya refutes a heretic's claim that the exile proves God's abandonment by arguing that the dispersion is actually a protective measure.

Ulla visits Pumbedita and initially mocks the cheapness of dates, but after suffering indigestion from eating them, he praises the Babylonians for their ability to study Torah while eating such difficult food.
Slaves of the king and queen slaughter two Paschal lambs, leading Rabban Gamliel to rule that the royals may eat from the first one while the sages abstain.
When a lizard is found in the royal kitchen, Rabban Gamliel instructs the staff to pour cold water on it, proving it is alive and thus preventing the meal from becoming impure.
A baraita records an incident where a father challenged his children to race to Jerusalem for the Paschal lamb, and the daughters arrived before the sons.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua attempts to share meals with Rav Pappa and later Ravina, but finds himself losing out due to their speed of eating, leading to a legal dispute and a humorous realization.
A Tanna recites a baraita regarding a Zava before Rav Adda bar Ahava, who challenges the validity of the text because a Zava cannot be ritually fit on her seventh day.
The Gemara cites the biblical account of Lot fleeing Sodom to calculate the distance an average person walks between dawn and sunrise.
Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai describes how a Divine Voice rebuked Nebuchadnezzar's hubris by informing him of the vast distances of the heavens and his ultimate descent to the pit.
Mareimar reports that he witnessed a tanna recite a baraita before Rav Pineḥas, who accepted the version as correct.

While dining in Akko as Shabbat begins, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel suggests interrupting the meal out of respect for Rabbi Yehuda, prompting a sharp rebuke from Rabbi Yosei and a final ruling on the matter.
Rabba bar Rav Huna visits the Exilarch and, when presented with a table as Shabbat begins, spreads a cloth to perform kiddush.
Rav Anan bar Taḥalifa recalls witnessing Shmuel descend from his roof to the ground floor and repeat the kiddush prayer to satisfy the requirement of eating in the place of the blessing.
When Rav Huna's lamp went out after kiddush, he moved his meal to his son Rabba's wedding house to eat in the light, necessitating a second kiddush.

Passage B describes a distinct set of recurring events involving different actors (Rabba and Abaye) and a specific interaction where Rabba instructs his students to eat, which constitutes a separate narrative unit from the event involving Rav Huna.
Rav Huna bar Yehuda visits Rava and observes his order of blessings for Havdala, leading to a legal challenge.
Rav Ya’akov bar Abba observes Rava reciting multiple blessings over wine during a meal and questions the necessity, leading Rava to explain his reasoning.

Rav Yeiva the Elder serves a group who first ask for a cup to recite Grace but then change their minds to drink more, only to be told by Rav Yeiva that their first statement legally concluded their meal.
While being served by Rav Aha, Ameimar, Mar Zutra, and Rav Ashi demonstrate three different ways of reciting blessings over wine during a meal, leading to a discussion of their reasons.
During a visit to Rava's house, Rav Ya’akov bar Abba observes and challenges the specific ways Rava and his attendant perform the Havdala ritual.
Rav Yehuda sends his son to observe Ulla's havdala, but the son sends Abaye instead, leading to a rebuke from Rav Yehuda when he finds out.
Rav Hananya and other students are eating before Shabbat and ask Rav Hamnuna to check the time, but he refuses based on his legal view of Shabbat's sanctity.
Rav Huna sees a man drinking water before Havdala and warns him that he is at risk of the ailment askara.
Rav Ashi visits Meḥoza and, unsure of what they call 'the Great Kiddush,' recites the standard blessing over wine and observes an old man's satisfied reaction to confirm he acted correctly.
Rav Yirmeya bar Abba accidentally eats before havdala at Rav Asi's house, leading Rav Asi to facilitate his havdala and explain the leniency to his questioning wife.
The sons of Rav Hisda report to Rav Ashi that when Ameimar visited them and they had no wine, he refused to use beer for havdala and fasted all night instead.
Levi sends a special date beer to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who tastes it and declares it worthy of being used for kiddush.
Rav Huna finds Rav reciting kiddush over beer and rebukes him by suggesting he is choosing a cheap drink to save money.
Abaye recounts how students crowded together on each other's knees to recline at Rabba's house, but were later told by Rav Yosef that they need not recline in his presence.
The Gemara describes how the mothers and attendants of Abaye and Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak would physically intervene with extra cups to ensure they never drank in dangerous pairs.
Rava allowed his students to leave after four cups, and even when Rava bar Livai was injured, Rava attributed the injury to a different cause rather than the danger of pairs.
Ameimar reports an encounter with the chief of witches who provided him with a protective incantation against witchcraft.
Rav Dimi of Neharde’a was careful not to mark barrels with even numbers, and once a barrel marked with pairs burst.
A man whose ex-wife tried to curse him daily was protected until he accidentally drank an even number of cups at her shop, allowing her witchcraft to work.
The Gemara alludes to an incident where Rabba bar Nahmani witnessed someone being harmed after drinking an even number of cups.
The Gemara alludes to an incident where a man riding a donkey was targeted by witchcraft despite certain conditions being met.
A demon mother warns her son to avoid a specific tree that killed his father, but the tree eventually kills the son as well.
A Torah scholar narrowly escapes a demon by fleeing after hearing it approach while he was near a caper-bush.
A city ruler is attacked by sixty demons after standing by a sorb tree, and a Sage's attempt to help with an amulet fails because he underestimated the number of demons.
While walking with his students, Abaye sees a demon and physically moves his companions to different sides to protect them from it.
While Rabbi Akiva is in prison, Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai visits him and successfully pressures him into teaching by threatening to involve the Roman authorities.
Rav Pappa enters a gentile woman's house to collect a debt and she invites him to sit on her bed, an incident used to explain a warning against sitting on such beds.
Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa encounters the demon queen Agrat and, after she threatens him, he uses his spiritual authority to restrict her presence to only two nights a week.
Abaye encounters the demon queen Agrat and decrees that she and her cohort may never pass through inhabited areas.
Rav tells his son Ayvu that since he failed to learn Torah, he should instead learn practical business advice.
When a baraita praising certain people is recited, Rav Safra becomes joyful thinking it refers to him, but Rava clarifies it refers to more pious individuals like Rav Hanina and Rav Oshaya.
Zigud testifies alone against Tuveya for a sin, but because a single witness cannot convict, Rav Pappa has Zigud lashed for defamation instead.
Ulla arrives in Babylonia and quotes a proverb about the social consequences of eating expensive versus cheap food.
Rava specifically sought out beets and rice for his Passover meal because he heard Rav Huna mention them as examples of the two cooked dishes.
While sitting at the Seder as a child, Abaye noticed the table being removed and asked why, leading Rabba to conclude that Abaye's curiosity exempted them from reciting 'Mah Nishtanah.'

Rav Naḥman asks his servant Daru what a freed slave should say to his master, and upon Daru's answer of praise, Rav Naḥman declares that they have already fulfilled the requirement to ask the Passover questions.
Mareimar inquires with the students of Rav Yosef and Rav Sheshet to discover that despite their blindness, they personally recited the Passover Haggadah.
Rav reports seeing a book of Psalms in his uncle's study hall where the word halleluya was split across two sides of a page.
Rabba would tell a joke to make the Sages laugh before beginning his lecture, at which point he would transition into a state of trepidation.
Rav Hisda reports seeing a book of Psalms where halleluya was written in the middle of a verse to prove it marks the end of a chapter.
Ulla bar Rav leads prayers before Rava using the Pumbedita formula, and Rava's silence is taken as a retraction of his previous legal stance.
Ravina recounts how a congregation in Sura tried to silence a prayer leader for using an unfamiliar formula, until Mareimar intervened to support the leader.
When God decrees that Adam will eat the herb of the field, Adam weeps and pleads not to be equated with his donkey.

Gabriel and Yurkamo petition God to descend and save Abraham and later Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah from the fiery furnaces of Nimrod and Nebuchadnezzar. Gabriel the angel receives permission from God to descend to the fiery furnace and subsequently recites a verse of praise.
God commands the Angel of the Sea to release the Egyptian bodies, and after a negotiation involving the Kishon River as a guarantor, the sea spews them out.
During Sisera's war, God uses the stars to drive the army into the Kishon River, which then sweeps them into the sea to fulfill its earlier guarantee.
When Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei falls ill, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi sends for his father's traditions, which Yishmael then transmits.
An eschatological narrative describing a great banquet where the patriarchs and leaders of Israel refuse to lead the blessing until David accepts the honor.
Abaye observes Rabba dozing during the eating of the matza and questions him, leading Rabba to define his state as 'dozing' to permit further eating.
Rabbi Simlai attends a redemption of a firstborn, is asked a legal question about the blessings, does not know the answer, and goes to the study hall to find out.
